experiences/aladura-babalola-revival/tit: Aladura revival and Joseph Babalola at Ilesa
experiences/aladura-babalola-revival/acc: Paraphrase of J.D.Y. Peel's reconstruction and church histories: Aladura ('people of prayer') groups arose in Yorubaland during the 1918 influenza epidemic, when Anglican members of the Precious Stone/Faith Tabernacle prayer society relied on prayer and blessed water. In July 1930, Joseph Ayo Babalola, a former steamroller driver who had reported a call in a vision (1928), began a revival at Oke-Oye, Ilesa: crowds came for healing by prayer and water, traditional objects were burned and thousands converted. Similar prophet-led churches include the Cherubim and Seraphim (from 1925) and the Church of the Lord (Aladura) (1930).
experiences/aladura-babalola-revival/con: Colonial authorities and mission churches were uneasy about mass healing meetings and conflict with the use of medicine; Babalola was briefly imprisoned in 1932 in connection with witch-finding activities. The movement led to the Christ Apostolic Church (1941), after a split with British Apostolic Church missionaries over the use of medicine.
experiences/aladura-babalola-revival/ass: The revival is a foundational sign of God's power in Africa; prayer, visions, fasting and holy water are central to worship.
Historically critical of rejection of medicine and syncretism concerns, while today acknowledging the Aladura as authentic African Christianity.
African Pentecostals see Aladura as forerunners, though newer Pentecostal churches often criticise Aladura use of candles, water and robes as syncretistic.
Peel interprets Aladura as a Yoruba search for power and well-being expressed in Christian form during colonial upheaval.
experiences/aladura-babalola-revival/sto:
In the early twentieth century south-western Nigeria, Yorubaland, was under British colonial rule, with Anglican, Methodist, Baptist and Catholic missions well established. In 1918 the global influenza pandemic struck hard. At St Saviour's Anglican Church in Ijebu-Ode, a group led by J.B. Shadare and the young woman Sophia Odunlami, claiming guidance through dreams and visions, formed a prayer circle that relied on prayer rather than medicine for healing. It became known as the Precious Stone (or Diamond) Society. Its members rejected both traditional medicine and Western medical treatment, and when the Anglican Church objected, the group left and affiliated in the 1920s with Faith Tabernacle, an American faith-healing church based in Philadelphia, through its magazine.

Joseph Ayo Babalola was born in 1904 and worked as a steamroller driver for the colonial Public Works Department. According to the Christ Apostolic Church's histories, in October 1928, while working on a road, he heard a voice calling him to leave his job and preach, and he received a vision commissioning him to pray for the sick using water blessed by prayer. He resigned, joined the Faith Tabernacle in Lagos, and began to preach.

In July 1930 Faith Tabernacle leaders gathered at Oke-Oye in Ilesa for a meeting. According to the church's tradition, during this gathering Babalola prayed for a dead boy who was then restored to life. Whatever the event, it marked the beginning of a mass movement. For weeks huge crowds came to Ilesa and then to other towns in Yoruba and Ekiti country to hear him preach and to be prayed for. People brought charms and traditional ritual objects to be burned, drank or washed in water he had prayed over, and testified to healings, especially of barrenness, blindness and lameness. Thousands were baptised. Missionaries and colonial officials reported that some mission churches lost members to the new movement.

Colonial authorities and mission churches watched with concern. They objected to the rejection of medicine and to fears of witchcraft accusations; in 1932 Babalola was imprisoned for some months in connection with witch-finding activities associated with the revival. Meanwhile the Faith Tabernacle leaders, seeking stronger links abroad, invited missionaries from the British Apostolic Church, a Pentecostal denomination based in Wales; they arrived in 1931. For several years the Nigerian movement and the British Pentecostals worked together, bringing Pentecostal teaching on Spirit baptism and tongues into the Yoruba revival.

Tensions grew, especially over medicine: some British missionaries used quinine against malaria, while many Nigerian leaders insisted on total reliance on prayer. Around 1939-40 the movement split. The British-linked group continued as the Apostolic Church, and Babalola and his Nigerian colleagues formed what was registered in the early 1940s as the Christ Apostolic Church, one of the largest indigenous Pentecostal churches in Nigeria. Babalola continued to preach until his death in 1959.

Alongside these developments other Aladura ('owners of prayer') churches arose, notably the Cherubim and Seraphim, founded in Lagos in 1925 by Moses Orimolade Tunolase and Christiana Abiodun Akinsowon, and the Church of the Lord (Aladura), founded by Josiah Oshitelu in 1930. They shared an emphasis on prayer, healing, visions and the struggle against evil spiritual powers, expressed in Yoruba forms of worship.
experiences/aladura-babalola-revival/key: During the influenza pandemic a prayer group at St Saviour's Anglican Church, Ijebu-Ode, begins healing by prayer alone.
The Cherubim and Seraphim movement is founded in Lagos by Moses Orimolade and Christiana Abiodun Akinsowon.
Steamroller driver Joseph Ayo Babalola reports a divine call and leaves his job to preach.
At Oke-Oye, Ilesa, Babalola begins a mass healing revival; crowds burn traditional objects.
Missionaries of the British Apostolic Church arrive at the invitation of Nigerian Faith Tabernacle leaders.
Babalola is imprisoned for some months in connection with witch-finding associated with the revival.
A split over the use of medicine leads Babalola's group to form what becomes the Christ Apostolic Church.
Babalola dies; the Christ Apostolic Church remains one of Nigeria's largest indigenous churches.
experiences/aladura-babalola-revival/sig: The Aladura movement and Babalola's revival created some of the first and largest African-initiated Pentecostal-type churches, and they helped set the pattern for Nigerian Christianity, now among the most vibrant in the world and a major exporter of churches to Europe and North America. They showed African Christians shaping the faith around their own concerns, especially healing, protection from evil powers and prophecy, which scholars such as J.D.Y. Peel and Lamin Sanneh interpret as genuine inculturation. Critics, including mission churches at the time, raised concerns about the rejection of medicine, witch-finding, and possible syncretism with traditional religion. Babalola is honoured today with a university and an annual pilgrimage at Ikeji-Arakeji.
experiences/east-african-revival/account: Paraphrase of Joe Church's memoir and later histories: after the Ugandan layman Simeon Nsibambi and the English missionary doctor Joe Church met in Kampala in 1929 and studied the Bible together, a revival broke out at the Gahini mission in Rwanda in 1933, then spread through Uganda, Kenya and Tanganyika. Its marks were conviction of sin, public confession, restitution and 'walking in the light' in fellowship. Some meetings in the 1930s saw people trembling, weeping and having visions, which leaders came to downplay.
experiences/east-african-revival/contemp: The revival largely stayed within the Anglican Church, though at times it clashed with clergy who found the Balokole ('saved ones') judgemental. During the Mau Mau emergency (1950s) many revivalists refused to take oaths and were killed, which gave the movement moral prestige.
experiences/east-african-revival/assessm: A formative renewal shaping East African Anglicanism and leaders such as Archbishop Janani Luwum and Festo Kivengere.
Sometimes claimed as a precursor, though the revival mainly avoided tongues and sought order within the established church.
Kevin Ward and Emma Wild-Wood stress its African leadership, interracial fellowship (Brethren) and its tensions with both mission and nationalist politics.
Public confession created strong community bonds and moral accountability, but some critics noted pressure and perfectionism.
experiences/east-african-revival/story:
In the 1920s the Church Missionary Society's Ruanda Mission, an evangelical Anglican mission rooted in the Keswick 'victorious life' tradition, opened stations in south-western Uganda and in Rwanda, then under Belgian mandate. At Gahini, on the eastern side of Rwanda, the mission ran a hospital and schools. Joe Church, a young English doctor from Cambridge, arrived there in 1927. In 1928-29 a severe famine struck Rwanda, and Church, exhausted and discouraged by the gap between the missionaries' message and the lives of many church members, travelled to Kampala in September 1929 for a break.

In Kampala he met Simeon Nsibambi, a Ugandan layman and government official known for his serious piety. According to Church's memoir, the two spent days studying the Bible together on the Holy Spirit and the victorious Christian life, and both reported a deep personal renewal. Nsibambi began to challenge fellow Christians in Kampala about sin and new life, and Church returned to Gahini with a new message.

Over the next few years a small group formed at Gahini, including Blasio Kigozi, Nsibambi's younger brother, a teacher at the mission, and Yosiya Kinuka, a hospital assistant. They met for prayer and Bible study and confessed sins to one another. In late 1933 and early 1934, according to Church and others, revival broke out at Gahini: people came under strong conviction of sin, wept, confessed publicly, and some trembled, cried out or had visions. Restitution followed: stolen goods were returned and enemies reconciled. Kigozi preached urgently to the church in Uganda but died of fever in January 1936.

Teams of Africans and Europeans, including Church, Nsibambi, William Nagenda and later Festo Kivengere, carried the message by conventions and visits through Uganda, Kenya, Tanganyika, Burundi and beyond. The movement's members came to be called the Balokole, 'the saved ones'. Their marks were open confession of sin, 'walking in the light' with one another in small fellowship groups, a strong emphasis on the cross and the blood of Jesus, simple living, and the hymn 'Tukutendereza Yesu' ('We praise you, Jesus'). Leaders came to discourage dramatic physical manifestations in favour of quiet brokenness and repentance.

The revival largely remained within the Anglican Church and other Protestant churches, but tensions were frequent. Clergy sometimes found the Balokole judgemental, separatist or contemptuous of church order, and revivalists criticised what they saw as nominal Christianity and compromise. In 1941 students at Bishop Tucker College, Mukono, were expelled after a dispute in which revivalists protested against what they saw as liberal teaching. Many Balokole also challenged ethnic and racial barriers, insisting that Europeans and Africans meet as equals in fellowship.

The movement's most dramatic test came in Kenya during the Mau Mau emergency of the 1950s. Many revival Christians among the Kikuyu refused to take Mau Mau oaths, which they saw as incompatible with their faith, while also refusing to take up arms for the colonial government; some were killed for their refusal. Their witness, combined with their opposition to colonial violence, gave the revival moral authority. The revival continued as a powerful current into the post-independence period, shaping leaders such as Archbishop Janani Luwum of Uganda, murdered under Idi Amin in 1977.

experiences/east-african-revival/signifi: The East African Revival is one of the longest-lasting and most influential revival movements in modern Christianity, shaping Anglican and Protestant churches in Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Kenya and Tanzania for decades and producing many of their leaders. It showed that revival could remain within an established church while renewing it through lay fellowship groups and African leadership, and its practice of mutual confession and reconciliation across racial lines was striking in colonial Africa. Critics have pointed to legalism, spiritual elitism and tendencies to schism, and later observers have asked why such a strong revival tradition did not prevent the violence of Rwanda in 1994. Its influence continues in East African Anglicanism and in global evangelical networks.
